title: A Winter for the Smile
premise: Isandro Zhou has spent twelve years as a hospice nurse listening to the dying count down to something no one names, keeping rituals — lights on, doors counted — that keep the counting out of his own head. When his childhood imaginary friend, a tall figure called Mister Winter, appears on his porch unchanged after thirty years, Isandro learns that in 1974 the town of Hollowmere took a child named Ada Reyes and let a man walk free, and that the town's borrowed years are running out. The countdown he hears in the dying is the town's own ledger coming due, and Mister Winter has come to collect — or to be paid. To survive, Isandro must uncover who really took Ada, return what was taken to the thing beneath the winter orchard, and choose between the town's survival and a justice the law never gave. In the end he gives the ledger a name instead of a child, the snow stops, and Isandro — the last one who remembers — keeps the lights on for no one, finally at peace.
about_author: Vesper Montrose is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who spent a decade in hospice wards across the Rust Belt before turning to writing. Their fiction draws on the small rituals of the dying and the quiet cruelties small towns agree to forget.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. On his night shift at Larkspur Hospice, a dying woman counts backwards from ninety and stops at zero with a smile that isn't hers. Isandro performs his rituals — lights on, doors counted — and we learn the counting has followed him for years. The emotional beat is weary dread: he manages the horror rather than understanding it.

chapters.title: Doors, Counted
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He drives home to Hollowmere through unseasonable snow, cataloguing the town's small wrongnesses: a shuttered orchard, a war memorial with one name scraped off. He checks his locks twice, three times. The beat is fragile control — a man whose life is a superstition he pretends is routine.

chapters.title: Mister Winter, Waiting
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. On the porch stands the tall gray figure from his childhood — Mister Winter, unchanged after thirty years, snow not touching him. He says only: 'The ledger is due, and you kept the best records.' Isandro slams the door; the counting starts inside his own head. The beat is the collapse of the wall between past and present.

chapters.title: What the Boy Agreed To
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, interleaved with fragmented memory. He recalls being seven, playing with Mister Winter in the orchard, and a promise he made and doesn't remember making. His mother's old box yields a 1974 newspaper clipping about a missing girl, Ada Reyes, and a man acquitted. The beat is dread deepening into obligation.

chapters.title: The Acquittal
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He visits retired deputy Harlan Voss, now dying in the hospice, who counts backwards and whispers fragments: the orchard, the sheriff, 'we let him go.' Voss's countdown accelerates whenever Isandro asks about Ada. The beat is the first glimpse that the town's guilt has a shape and a name.

chapters.title: Snow in July Rooms
chapters.summary: Alternating Isandro and Mister Winter's POV. Mister Winter moves through Hollowmere's homes unseen, standing over the original 1974 witnesses as they sleep, and the snow follows him indoors. Isandro, meanwhile, finds frost on the inside of his windows. The beat is invasion — the past no longer confined to memory.

chapters.title: The Reyes House
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He visits the abandoned Reyes house and meets Marisol Reyes, Ada's niece, who returned to settle the estate and has been dreaming of an orchard in winter. She shows him Ada's drawings: a tall gray figure, a counting game. The beat is alliance — two people realizing they were both chosen.

chapters.title: Ledger of the Living
chapters.summary: Isandro and Marisol's POV. In the county archive they find that eleven people connected to Ada's case have died in the past year — each after a documented countdown, each smiling at the end. The last name on the list hasn't died yet. The beat is the horror becoming arithmetic, a debt with a schedule.

chapters.title: The Man Who Walked
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The acquitted man, Dale Pruett, is alive, elderly, and living openly in Hollowmere, beloved, a deacon. When Isandro confronts him, Pruett smiles with a smile that isn't his and says, 'He already took my turn. Ask what I gave.' The beat is revulsion and the first hint that guilt has been traded like currency.

chapters.title: What Pruett Gave
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, digging into Pruett's past. She learns Pruett's own son vanished in 1975, a year after Ada, and the case was never opened. Pruett gave the town a child to stop the counting — and the town accepted. The beat is moral vertigo: the horror isn't one man, it's the arithmetic everyone agreed to.

chapters.title: Harlan's Zero
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Voss reaches zero at the hospice, and in his last minute he lucidly confesses: the sheriff buried the evidence, the town voted in a church basement, and Ada is under the winter orchard. He dies smiling, and the frost on Isandro's windshield forms the number nine. The beat is grief braided with fury — testimony at last, and a deadline.

chapters.title: Nine
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The countdown has transferred to the town: nine days. Power flickers, the snow stops melting, and residents begin counting in their sleep. The sheriff's grandson begs Isandro to stop digging. The beat is siege — the town itself now the dying patient.

chapters.title: The Orchard in Winter
chapters.summary: Isandro and Marisol's POV. They dig at the orchard at night and find a root-cellar door that wasn't there, breathing cold. Mister Winter appears and explains the ledger: the thing beneath was wronged in 1974, and it counts what it is owed. The beat is awe and terror — the monster is a creditor, not a predator.

chapters.title: The Wronged
chapters.summary: Mister Winter's POV. Through him we see the thing beneath the orchard as it was: a child, Ada, taken by Pruett, her death witnessed by the town's silence — and something older in the ground that took her grievance as its own. The beat is tragic reversal: the horror is grief with a ledger.

chapters.title: The Church Basement Vote
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She finds the 1974 minutes hidden in the church records: eleven names, a unanimous vote to stay silent, and a line about 'the arrangement.' One name is Isandro's grandfather. The beat is betrayal — the debt runs through Isandro's own bloodline.

chapters.title: Grandfather's Room
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. In his late grandfather's locked room he finds the original evidence Pruett's defense buried — Ada's shoe, photographs — and a letter: 'If it ever counts to you, give it what we took. Not another child. The truth, and the man.' The beat is inheritance reframed: Isandro was chosen to finish, not to pay.

chapters.title: Four
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. With four days left, Pruett is found frozen alive in his pew, counting, smiling, begging Isandro to give the ledger 'someone else.' The town turns on Isandro and Marisol, blaming them for waking it. The beat is isolation — justice and survival pulling in opposite directions.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Mister Winter's POV. The thing beneath offers Isandro the old bargain: give it a guilty life and the town is spared, the ledger resets for another fifty years. It shows him Ada, still counting, still waiting to be found. The beat is temptation — the easy cruelty that started everything, offered again.

chapters.title: Two
chapters.summary: Isandro and Marisol's POV. Isandro refuses the bargain and instead prepares to give the ledger what his grandfather's letter demanded: the truth spoken publicly, the evidence surrendered, Pruett's living body as witness. Marisol stands with him before a town that wants them gone. The beat is resolve — justice chosen over arithmetic.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Names
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. In the snowbound town square, Isandro reads the 1974 minutes aloud, names the eleven, names Pruett, names Ada, and lays the evidence and Pruett — still counting — at the orchard door. The ground opens. The beat is climax: testimony as payment, the town forced to hear what it voted to forget.

chapters.title: Zero
chapters.summary: Mister Winter's POV, closing on Isandro. Ada stops counting and is carried up out of the cold; the thing beneath takes Pruett's confessed name instead of a child, and the ledger closes. Mister Winter, his purpose spent, begins to fade — and thanks Isandro for keeping the records all these years. The beat is release and farewell.

chapters.title: A Winter for the Smile
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Spring comes wrong-footed and clean; the snow melts all at once, the orchard blooms, and a small marker for Ada Reyes appears with the town's reluctant, official apology. Isandro returns to the hospice, where the dying no longer count — they only say a name and smile. He keeps the lights on out of habit, and for the first time, out of peace.
